name: LAMBADA
description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. The dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages extracted from novels.
creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
publisher: CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam
citeAs: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández. 2016. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. arXiv:1606.06031v1 [cs.CL]
rai:dataCollection: LAMBADA consists of passages composed of a context (on average 4.6 sentences) and a target sentence. The context size is the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens. The task is to guess the last word of the target sentence (the target word). The data come from the Book Corpus containing unpublished novels. The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The corpus contains unpublished novels to minimize the potential usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources for the task. After duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, the corpus contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Passages were filtered to reduce time and cost of dataset collection by excluding passages that are relatively easy for standard language models. A combination of four language models was used (a pre-trained RNN, a standard 4-gram model, an RNN, and a feed-forward model trained on the Book Corpus). Any passage whose target word had probability 0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The novels were randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. The corpus underwent duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list. Passages were filtered using four language models to exclude relatively easy cases. The LAMBADA dataset was further split between development and testing using the same novel-based division method.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A random sample of the remaining passages were evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: (1) one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if the guess was right, (2) a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if that guess was also right, (3) more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset. The subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence. It was ensured that the same subject could not judge the same item in both passage and sentence conditions. The criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: two consecutive subjects had to exactly match the missing word, and no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2 and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all the selection steps. The strict hit-or-miss approach was used, keeping only items that can be unambiguously determined by human subjects, requiring perfect match rather than plausible or synonymous continuations.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Step 1: 1 annotator; Step 2: 1 additional annotator (2 total); Step 3: up to 10 annotators attempting to guess based on sentence context only
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models were used for filtering: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN), a standard 4-gram model, an RNN trained on the Book Corpus, and a feed-forward model trained on the Book Corpus
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/. The test set will be made available at the time of the competition. A public competition based on the LAMBADA data is planned.
rai:dataSocialImpact: LAMBADA is meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. The dataset aims to test language models on their ability to take a broad discourse context into account when predicting a word, addressing the limitation of systems that can locally produce sensible language fragments but fail to take the meaning of the broader discourse context into account.
rai:dataBiases: More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context, while in the input data that was the case for less than 15% of the passages. Most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and verbs (7.7%). Proper nouns are hugely over-represented in LAMBADA, while other categories are under-represented compared to the POS distribution in the input. The LAMBADA items contain quoted direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% of LAMBADA items vs. 61% of items in the input sample).
rai:dataLimitations: The constraint that the target word be the last word of the sentence, while not necessary for the research goal, makes the task more natural for human subjects. The strict perfect-match approach was used due to practical and methodological challenges in determining which answers other than the original fit the passage well. Cost considerations precluded using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve the quality of filtering. The dataset was designed to challenge language models with harder-than-average examples where broad context understanding is crucial. Standard language models are bound to fail on LAMBADA by design, as one of the first filters was to choose passages where a number of simple language models were failing to predict the upcoming word.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for testing language models on their ability to understand broad discourse context. The training data (203 million words from 2,662 novels) can be used to train general-purpose language models. The development data can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of the LAMBADA passages. LAMBADA is proposed as a challenging test set meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. The dataset casts language understanding in the classic word prediction framework of language modeling.
